articles.title: Sculpt & Edit launches wellness clinic after founder builds business from scratch
articles.excerpt: Sculpt & Edit founder Amy has opened a new wellness clinic after finding herself without a job and turning that moment into an opportunity to build her own treatment business, with a focus on lymphatic drainage, post-surgery support and body treatments.
articles.content_html:
A new wellness clinic, Sculpt & Edit, has opened with a focus on treatments designed around body confidence, recovery and wellbeing.

Founder Amy said the clinic is intended to offer an alternative to a traditional beauty salon, bringing together lymphatic drainage and post-surgery support with body contouring and sculpting treatments.

The clinic will also offer more holistic treatments including Reiki and reflexology, alongside a growing focus on skin health and hydration. Amy said vitamin injections and IV wellness treatments will also form part of the clinic's offering.

The launch follows a significant career change for Amy, who found herself without a job at the beginning of 2026 and decided to take the risk of building a business of her own.

Over the following eight months, she has developed Sculpt & Edit from the ground up, initially through her treatment business before moving into a physical wellness clinic.

She described the opening of the clinic as a major milestone after what she said had been a life-changing year, and hopes her experience will encourage other people considering starting their own business.

Sculpt & Edit is now welcoming clients at the new clinic, with further information about treatments and the business available directly from the clinic.

articles.title: Rochdale’s Breaking Barriers secures core funding to expand its cultural work across Greater Manchester
articles.excerpt: Rochdale-based production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of GMCA core funding to expand cultural programmes, paid opportunities and creative development across Greater Manchester.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale-based multidisciplinary production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of core funding from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to strengthen the organisation and expand its cultural programmes across the region.

Over the funding period, Breaking Barriers plans to offer 42 paid placements through its Young Company programme, giving creatives aged 18–25 hands-on experience working on professional arts productions.

It will also provide 328 paid freelance roles and 45 in-kind artist residencies at its Rochdale base at Richard Street Studios.

Young Company participants will gain practical skills in producing, sound design, filmmaking and direction, with a focus on young people from underrepresented backgrounds who have had fewer opportunities to get into the arts.

A producer development programme will also support 36 creative producers a year to develop their own projects, secure resources and build sustainable careers.

Awarded through the Spirit strand of the GMCA Culture Fund, the investment will support Breaking Barriers to continue delivering theatre, film and immersive outdoor artworks, alongside training, mentoring and paid opportunities for emerging creatives.

Parvez Qadir, Artistic Director of Breaking Barriers, said: “Three years of core funding gives us the stability to plan ahead and grow as a company here in Rochdale. There’s so much creative talent locally, and we can now give more young people paid opportunities to work alongside experienced artists on our productions. It also enables us to keep building partnerships across Greater Manchester and develop projects shaped by local people, bringing their stories to life.”

Bev Craig, Mayor of Greater Manchester, said: “Culture has the power to connect communities, inspire creativity and strengthen pride in the places we call home.

“Through the Greater Manchester Culture Fund, we're investing in a diverse range of cultural organisations that help make our city region such a vibrant and inclusive place to live. Breaking Barriers is a fantastic example of a local company creating opportunities for young people to share their stories, develop their creativity and shape cultural experiences on their doorstep.”

Projects are currently planned to span the boroughs of Rochdale, Bury, Salford, Stockport, Manchester, Tameside and Bolton over three years.

Residents and local communities will help create outdoor artworks using sound, projection and light, alongside films and digital storytelling projects reflecting local experiences.

The funding will also help sustain and expand Breaking Barriers’ theatre in education work.

This includes multi-partnership delivery of Crossing the Line, a theatre and workshop programme tackling child criminal exploitation, which has already reached more than 15,000 young people across more than 220 schools.

Blind Side, exploring violence against women and girls, consent and healthy relationships, will continue to tour. Support from the Spirit strand will enable more time and resources to further expand its reach into other boroughs.

Source: Breaking Barriers.

articles.title: Rochdale's 'Kenion Street' Album Celebrates Local Music Heritage
articles.excerpt: The 'Kenion Street' album, featuring local artists' renditions of iconic tracks, has gained national radio attention, highlighting Rochdale's rich musical history.
articles.content_html:
An album titled 'Kenion Street', celebrating the musical heritage of Rochdale, has gained significant traction, reaching millions of listeners on national radio and thousands more on streaming platforms. Released this summer as part of Rochdale's designation as Greater Manchester Town of Culture, the album features local artists performing their interpretations of classic tracks originally recorded at the borough's renowned Cargo and Suite Sixteen studios.

The album includes 11 tracks, such as PoolEra's rendition of OMD's 'Electricity', Medley's version of New Order's 'Dreams Never End', and Jennifer Read's cover of The Fall's 'Totally Wired'. These new recordings were produced by Jamie Alsop at Voltalab Sound Studios, located in the original Cargo/Suite Sixteen building on Kenion Street. This site has a rich history, having hosted legendary artists like Joy Division, The Stone Roses, and Happy Mondays between 1977 and 2001.

The album has received notable airplay, with K-Estate's version of Gang of Four's 'Damaged Goods' being featured on BBC Radio 6 Music and named Track of the Day on Radio X. Other tracks have been played across various stations, including XS Manchester and Mersey Radio, contributing to a combined audience of over 3.5 million listeners. Listening parties for the album were also held at Rough Trade shops in cities such as London, Liverpool, and Nottingham, with vinyl copies distributed to record shops nationwide.

The release of 'Kenion Street' not only showcases local talent but also reinforces Rochdale's status as a significant player in the music industry, celebrating its historical contributions and inspiring future generations of artists.

articles.title: Rochdale Council to Consider Motion to Lift Restrictions on Former Pubs
articles.excerpt: Councillors will discuss a motion aimed at removing restrictions that prevent former pubs from reopening as public houses, following the closure of the Wheatsheaf in Littleborough.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to consider a motion on Thursday, 13 October, that seeks to lift restrictions preventing former pubs from reopening as public houses. The motion, proposed by Councillor Richard Jackson, comes in response to the recent closure of the Wheatsheaf pub in Littleborough, a Grade II-listed building that has been a local fixture since the 18th century.

Councillor Jackson's motion highlights the impact of restrictive covenants imposed by pub-owning companies when they sell former pub buildings. These covenants often prevent future owners from using the premises for the sale of alcohol or as a public house, effectively locking communities out of the opportunity to revive their local pubs. The Wheatsheaf's closure has sparked significant local interest in preserving and potentially reopening the establishment, possibly through community ownership.

The motion also references the loss of the former Royal Oak pub in Littleborough, which was converted into a shop selling various goods after being unable to operate as a pub due to similar restrictions. Councillor Jackson argues that such practices have detrimental effects on local heritage and community cohesion.

If the motion is approved, it could pave the way for former pubs in the borough to be revitalised, allowing communities to reclaim these spaces for social use. The council's decision will be closely watched by local residents and stakeholders invested in the future of their community pubs.

articles.title: Plans for Direct Train Services from Rochdale to London Rejected by Rail Regulator
articles.excerpt: The Office of Rail and Road has rejected proposals for new direct train services between Rochdale and London Euston, citing capacity issues on the West Coast Main Line.
articles.content_html:
Plans to introduce direct train services from Rochdale to London Euston have been rejected by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) due to concerns over capacity on the West Coast Main Line. The ORR stated that the line is already under significant pressure, and adding more services could lead to increased delays and cancellations for passengers.

Lumo Trains had submitted an application for up to four daily return services between Rochdale and the capital, aiming to enhance connectivity for local residents. However, the ORR's analysis indicated that the existing timetable lacks the necessary gaps to accommodate additional trains without compromising the reliability of the network.

This decision follows a similar rejection in 2025, highlighting ongoing challenges in expanding rail services in the region. The ORR emphasised the importance of maintaining current service reliability, stating that gaps in the timetable are crucial for allowing trains to recover from disruptions. Stephanie Tobyn, director of strategy, policy and reform at ORR, noted that while new services could benefit passengers, the current state of the West Coast Main Line does not allow for such expansions without risking overall service reliability.

While the proposed Rochdale services were turned down, the ORR did approve one additional evening service from London to Chester, which will help improve service efficiency without adding to the congestion on the West Coast Main Line. articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The narrow gorge known as the Thrutch has a real rock niche called the Fairies’ Chapel and a long written tradition of fairy and witch stories — but the fairies themselves belong to folklore, not the official record.
articles.summary: The narrow gorge known as the Thrutch has a real rock niche called the Fairies’ Chapel and a long written tradition of fairy and witch stories — but the fairies themselves belong to folklore, not the official record.
articles.body:
Healey Dell is one of Rochdale borough’s best‑loved beauty spots: a wooded, rocky cleft through which the River Spodden runs beneath the Victorian viaduct, past the remains of old mills and into a shallow pool with an overhanging rock niche commonly called the Fairies’ Chapel. The site is a managed nature reserve with a heritage centre and public access, and its landscape — stone, river and industrial archaeology — is verifiable and recorded by local authorities. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The documented history is straightforward. Healey Dell contains the remains of nineteenth‑century millworks and a late Victorian railway viaduct; these features and the hollowed rock forms are explained by local industrial development, river erosion and historic floods rather than supernatural causes. Archaeological and heritage surveys used by local managers underpin the reserve’s interpretation and the viaduct and mill remains are part of the borough’s recorded historic environment. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/heritage-gateway/results/record/40b1668f-44ca-471f-970f-e86d7ea4f9ac/MGM3098))

The idea of a “Fairies’ Chapel” at the pool and rock niche is older than modern tourism and appears in nineteenth‑century collections of Lancashire tradition. The most influential printed source is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire, published in the 1829–31 period, which gathers local romances about fairies, a small “Healey Dwarf,” witches and enchanted meetings in the Thrutch; Roby’s telling helped fix many story elements that later writers retold. There are also later local poems and pamphlets that dramatised the Chapel as a meeting place for a Fairy Queen and supernatural events. These accounts are literary and folkloric sources, not archival evidence of supernatural events. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Local interpretation today treats those tales as folklore. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre and the volunteer guides present the Fairies’ Chapel stories as part of the Dell’s cultural history, using nineteenth‑century tales, local recollections and creative retellings to entertain visitors while also pointing to the real natural and industrial features that inspired them. The centre’s printed guides and on‑site materials identify the Healey Dwarf and the fairy queen narratives as tradition rather than objective history. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

What the record cannot show is the presence of supernatural beings. There is no official, documentary evidence that “fairies,” witches with magical powers, or a Fairy King ever existed in a factual sense; such claims belong to oral tradition, poetry and folklore. Where nineteenth‑century collectors recorded striking tales — a miller led to the Chapel by an enchanted hare, witches turned to stone, or a small stone figure acting as guardian — they were transcribing local belief and imaginative storytelling rather than court records, land deeds or contemporary administrative reports. If a claim cannot be verified by archival or scientific sources, it should be described plainly as legend. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

That clear separation matters for how we value the site. The Fairies’ Chapel is culturally significant: the stories illuminate local language, nineteenth‑century folk collecting, tourism tastes and how communities frame landscape meaning. They are also useful to the heritage centre and schools as a way to engage children with geology, river processes and industrial history. But if you come to Healey Dell hoping to meet a literal Fairy Queen, the official record and heritage interpretation will politely tell you that the fairies are part of the Dell’s long imaginative life, not its archaeological inventory. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

For locals and visitors, the best answer is both simple and satisfying: the Chapel is real; the stories are real; the fairies are part of folklore. Whether you treat the tales as playful local theatre, cultural heritage, or something you might believe in privately is up to you — but the borough’s records, historic surveys and the heritage centre make a clear distinction between documented fact and the wonderful, well‑documented world of Lancashire legend. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/heritage-gateway/results/record/40b1668f-44ca-471f-970f-e86d7ea4f9ac/MGM3098))

articles.title: Mayor Faisal Rana visits Rochdale Sixth Form College to see student support and results
articles.excerpt: Mayor Faisal Rana and the Mayoress visited Rochdale Sixth Form College, highlighting its student support, pastoral provision and recent academic achievements.
articles.content_html: Mayor Faisal Rana and the Mayoress have visited Rochdale Sixth Form College, meeting Principal Karl Smith and touring the college to see its facilities and student support. The visit included the Achievement Centre, which provides additional support for students who may be falling behind or need extra help with their studies. The Mayor and Mayoress also visited the student café and highlighted the college's focus on pastoral support, attendance and punctuality. ### College results and progression Rochdale Sixth Form College says its students achieved strong results in 2026. The college's website describes it as one of the country's strongest sixth form colleges for student progress, while its latest results announcement reported exceptional A-level and BTEC outcomes. The college also says around 80% of its students progress to higher education and that it has retained an Outstanding Ofsted judgement. The college's website currently highlights students progressing to Oxford and Cambridge, including former Oulder Hill student Joseph, who achieved three A*s and an A* in his EPQ before progressing to Cambridge, and former Hollingworth student Summer, who achieved four A*s and an A* in her EPQ before progressing to Oxford. Faisal Rana said the visit was particularly meaningful because four of his children had attended the college and achieved what he described as exceptional results. He said the visit offered a different perspective on the college, beyond that of a parent. He also praised the college's emphasis on supporting students, raising aspirations and creating opportunities for young people in the borough. Principal Karl Smith hosted the visit. Source: Faisal Rana, Mayor of Rochdale; Rochdale Sixth Form College. articles.title: RBH football team takes part in Housing Association Charity Cup 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing colleagues took part in the Housing Association Charity Cup 2026 after weeks of training, with the team already looking ahead to next year's tournament.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing's football team joined eight other housing providers for the Housing Association Charity Cup 2026 at Goals Manchester.

The tournament followed weeks of preparation from RBH colleagues, who gave up their own time to train every Wednesday at the Soccer Factory in Castleton.

While Team RBH did not bring home the trophy, the organisation said the tournament was a successful opportunity for colleagues to come together and enjoy some friendly competition.

Salix Homes won the 2026 cup, while RBH congratulated everyone who took part and represented the organisation.

### Looking ahead to next year

RBH thanked Chris Hudspith, its Multi Trade Co-ordinator, for arranging the training sessions and encouraging colleagues to get involved.

Hudspith said the football programme had been a positive experience and an opportunity to meet people from other teams and departments while taking part in a shared interest.

Martin Platt, an IT Trainer, said the team came away from the tournament feeling that some close games could have gone differently, adding that they hoped to return next year and win the trophy.

RBH also said it is hoping to have a women's team competing in next year's tournament.

articles.title: Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit highlights opportunities for local businesses
articles.excerpt: Businesses and organisations gathered at the Crown Oil Arena for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on accessing contracts, bidding and local economic growth.
articles.content_html:
Businesses and organisations from across the borough have come together for the Rochdale Procurement 360 Summit, with discussions focused on how local firms can access procurement opportunities and grow their businesses.

The event was organised by the Rochdale Development Agency and held at the newly refurbished Crown Oil Arena, home of Rochdale AFC.

The summit brought together organisations involved in procurement, regeneration and business support, including STAR Procurement, Match My Project, Hopwood Hall College, Willmott Dixon and the Rochdale Development Agency.

Discussions focused on how businesses can get onto the procurement ladder, understand the bidding process and position themselves to compete for contracts and opportunities with larger organisations.

Mayor Faisal Rana, who attended the event, said greater collaboration between local businesses and organisations delivering investment across the borough was important to ensuring local firms can benefit from upcoming opportunities.

He highlighted figures from the Rochdale Development Agency's latest independent economic impact assessment, which it says found that its work had created, supported or safeguarded 765 jobs and supported 699 businesses. The assessment also reported £14.30 in local economic value for every £1 invested.

The mayor also pointed to major investment programmes including Atom Valley, the Rochdale Rail Corridor, town centre regeneration, housing and skills investment as areas where businesses could potentially benefit from future procurement and supply-chain opportunities.

The summit comes as public-sector and regeneration projects continue to create demand for contractors, suppliers and other local businesses across a range of sectors.

The Rochdale Development Agency and organisations involved in procurement are encouraging businesses to understand the opportunities available and build their capacity to bid for work.

The event also underlined the potential economic impact of keeping a greater share of investment within the local economy, through jobs, business growth and local supply chains.

The Rochdale AFC Community Trust was also associated with the event.

articles.title: Syke granted Conservation Area status to protect its historic character
articles.excerpt: Syke has been granted Conservation Area status by Rochdale Borough Council, following a consultation in which 33 of 38 responses supported the designation.
articles.content_html:
Syke has been granted Conservation Area status by Rochdale Borough Council, with the designation intended to protect the area's architectural and historic character from unsympathetic development.

The council confirmed the designation on 17 February 2026, describing Syke as an area with a unique and rich history. It highlighted the area's position on a historic packhorse route and its traditional weavers' cottages, including buildings with distinctive upper-floor windows designed to maximise natural light before electricity became widespread.

The Syke Conservation Area Appraisal provides further historical detail. It identifies Syke Road as part of the historic packhorse route linking Clitheroe with Rochdale and beyond, and records a network of historic paths across the Common, including remnants of the old packhorse trail.

The designated area covers Syke Common, parts of Dewhirst Road and Syke Road, and sections of Buckley Wood. The appraisal also identifies the northern extent of Cronkeyshaw Common and Syke Pond, well-preserved weavers' cottages, evidence of former industry, vernacular buildings and farmsteads, sandstone buildings, dry-stone and flagstone walls, and historic views and paths.

The appraisal includes historic maps from 1851, 1891, 1911 and 1936, alongside sections covering architectural character, historic buildings, key views and vistas, green spaces and the area's overall character. It provides the documented basis for the council's assessment of Syke's special architectural and historic interest.

### Public support for the designation

Rochdale Borough Council said more than 85% of locals backed the proposals. The consultation records 38 responses, of which 33 were positive about Conservation Area status for Syke. That represents approximately 87% of respondents, although the total number of responses was relatively small.

The responses nevertheless provide evidence of strong support among those who took part, as well as an indication that local heritage was an important consideration for respondents.

Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for regeneration, described the designation as a worthy addition to Rochdale's existing Conservation Areas and highlighted local engagement and pride in Syke's heritage.

### What Conservation Area status means

Conservation Areas are designated by local authorities where an area has special architectural or historic interest. Historic England guidance also provides for local authorities to prepare Conservation Area Appraisals setting out an area's character and significance.

The Syke appraisal states that its purpose is to explain the area's significance and identify measures to preserve and enhance its special character. It is intended to guide future development and inform future management plans. The document was prepared following consultation with local residents and draws on site visits, archive material, information from residents and Historic England guidance.

Historic England told Rochdale Daily that it had no involvement in the designation of the new Syke Conservation Area and directed us to its general guidance on Conservation Areas. Council documents show that Historic England guidance and documentation were considered during the process, but the designation itself was determined locally.

### Planning protections and what is not yet established

Conservation Area status introduces additional considerations within the planning process and can make permitted development rights more restrictive. The appraisal identifies circumstances where planning permission may be required, including substantial demolition of buildings or structures and certain works involving walls, gates, fences, extensions and alterations.

Article 4 Directions can remove further permitted development rights, but they are not automatic consequences of Conservation Area designation. The available information does not establish that an Article 4 Direction has been introduced for Syke.

The practical effect on individual properties will therefore depend on the planning controls that apply and any further decisions made by Rochdale Borough Council. The designation provides a framework for protecting Syke's special character, while the appraisal sets out the evidence and management considerations underpinning it.

articles.title: Man arrested on suspicion of murder after man found deceased on Curzon Road
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Police has arrested a man on suspicion of murder after a man was found deceased at an address on Curzon Road, Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder following the death of a man at an address on Curzon Road, Rochdale.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers received a report of a concern for the welfare of a man at an address on Curzon Road at around 7.55pm on Wednesday 7 October 2026.

Emergency services attended and the man was sadly confirmed deceased at the scene.

A man in his 40s has been arrested on suspicion of murder and remains in police custody for questioning.

GMP said an investigation is underway to establish the circumstances surrounding the death and that detectives are exploring all lines of enquiry.

The man's next of kin have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

Detective Superintendent Richard Hunt said: “Firstly, our thoughts remain with the family of the man who sadly died, and we have officers assigned to support them through this difficult time.

“An investigation is underway and officers are working at pace to establish the circumstances which led to this man’s death.

“We currently have a man in custody for questioning and ask the public to refrain from speculating at this time. This is a live investigation, and we are currently exploring all avenues of enquiry and keeping an open mind.”

No finding of guilt should be inferred from an arrest or allegation. The arrested man remains under investigation and is presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

articles.title: Sara Rowbotham: the Rochdale health worker who raised 181 safeguarding alerts
articles.excerpt: Sara Rowbotham repeatedly raised concerns about vulnerable young people while working for Rochdale’s Crisis Intervention Team, later giving evidence to Parliament about the response to child sexual exploitation in the town.
articles.content_html:
Sara Rowbotham became one of the most recognisable figures associated with the response to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale after repeatedly raising concerns about vulnerable young people while working for the town’s NHS Crisis Intervention Team.

Rowbotham worked as the Crisis Intervention Team Co-ordinator and Sexual Health Improvement Specialist. The team was established in 2004 and supported thousands of young people, including those who disclosed concerns about sexual abuse and exploitation.

In evidence to the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee in November 2012, Rowbotham told MPs that, over a period covering the years from 2005 to 2011, her team had identified referrals involving 103 young people.

She also told the committee that she had made 181 alerts to Children’s Social Care about concerns involving young people.

Asked whether she believed police and social services had worked together effectively, Rowbotham said this had happened “very rarely” in the early period and that she had subsequently begun making the Safeguarding Children Unit aware of the referrals so that strategy meetings could be convened.

The committee also heard evidence from other senior officials about the handling of the information. The subsequent Home Affairs Committee report described missed opportunities and examined the response of children's social care and police to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale.

Rowbotham told MPs that she had repeatedly tried to make protective services aware of the vulnerability of young people and that she believed agencies had failed to provide a sufficiently comprehensive and coordinated response.

The evidence came after the prosecution of nine men in Rochdale in 2012 for serious sexual offences against girls. The case prompted wider scrutiny of how authorities had responded to reports of child sexual exploitation.

Rowbotham continued to speak publicly about the response. In 2014, she was made redundant from her role. Contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian documented her concerns about the handling of the case and the impact of losing her position.

Her story later reached a much wider audience when the BBC drama Three Girls was broadcast in May 2017, with Maxine Peake portraying Rowbotham.

A petition calling for Rowbotham to be formally recognised attracted more than 100,000 signatures within days of the programme airing and ultimately exceeded 275,000 signatures, according to contemporary reports.

Rowbotham subsequently entered local politics. She was elected as a councillor for North Middleton in 2015 and went on to serve as Deputy Leader of Rochdale Borough Council and as a cabinet member.

Her public recognition also continued. She received a Special Recognition Award at the NHS Heroes Awards in 2018 and was made an honorary member of the NSPCC Council that year. In 2021, she was appointed MBE for services to young people.

Rowbotham’s evidence to Parliament remains part of the official record of the scrutiny that followed the Rochdale child sexual exploitation cases. Her account of the 181 alerts, and questions about how information held by frontline services was acted upon, formed part of the wider examination of safeguarding failures in the town.

articles.title: New Awaab’s Law protections could cover millions more renters and vulnerable households
articles.excerpt: A government consultation will examine extending Awaab’s Law to private renters and other accommodation, with faster legal deadlines for landlords to tackle serious hazards such as damp and mould.
articles.content_html:
Millions more households could receive stronger legal protections against dangerous housing conditions under plans to extend Awaab’s Law beyond social housing.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government has launched a consultation on how the law could be introduced for private renters and whether similar protections should apply to other forms of accommodation.

Awaab’s Law currently provides legal deadlines for social landlords to investigate and address serious hazards, including dangerous damp and mould. The measures were introduced in memory of two-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in 2020 after prolonged exposure to damp and mould in his home.

The proposed extension could mean around nine million households are covered by new repair timescales, compared with around four million currently covered.

The consultation is considering protections for private rented homes as well as:

temporary accommodation for homeless people and families;

accommodation for young people leaving care; and

supported housing, including accommodation used by older, disabled and other vulnerable people.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said all renters should be able to expect a safe and decent home, regardless of tenure.

“Awaab’s Law is already helping to drive up standards in the social housing sector. We’re now moving to extend it to private landlords so that England’s 11 million private renters can enjoy the same protections,” he said.

The government says landlords are already required to act when serious hazards are identified. Around one in 10 private rented homes is estimated to contain a Category 1 hazard, the most serious level.

The Renters’ Rights Act has also introduced fines of up to £7,000 where serious dangers are found. Awaab’s Law would add legally defined timescales requiring action on the most serious conditions.

The consultation will help determine how Awaab’s Law should operate in the private rented sector, including the timescales for the new protections to come into force. It closes on 18 December 2026.

Generation Rent welcomed the move. Chief Executive Holly Williamson said too many renters live in homes that can harm their health and wait months for landlords to address problems.

Crisis also backed the proposals, highlighting the conditions faced by people living in temporary accommodation, including hostels and bed and breakfasts.

The Renters’ Reform Coalition said nobody should have to live in a home that makes them ill or puts their life at risk, while Independent Age said older renters can face serious problems including rats and mould and may be afraid to request repairs.

Independent Age said almost 96% of older renters it polled supported Awaab’s Law.

Become, the national charity for children in care and young care leavers, also welcomed the government’s consideration of stronger standards for accommodation used by young people leaving care.

The proposals form part of commitments in the Renters’ Rights Act and the National Plan to End Homelessness.

The government says the changes are intended to ensure dangerous housing conditions are dealt with quickly and that tenants can raise concerns without fear of repercussions.

Source: Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government.

The Open Day will take place at the Trackside Bar at Bury Bolton Street Station from 10am to 3pm on Monday 12 October.
